title: Worried about the AI bubble popping? How investing pros say to adjust your strategy
description: Recent headlines coming out of the technology sector may have some investors feeling queasy. Shares of Nvidia, the firm whose chips have powered much
body: Recent headlines coming out of the technology sector may have some investors feeling queasy. Shares of Nvidia, the firm whose chips have powered much of the artifical intelligence boom, are down 35% since their high on October 6. Part of the downdraft came after company co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO amid revelations of his romantic ties to a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy.All told, tech companies in the S&P 500 are down nearly 17% from their early October highs, which has many investors wondering: Is the AI bubble we've all been hearing about finally ready to pop? "People have been worried for awhile that we have a tech-heavy, top-heavy market that's overly focused on a single theme," says Dan Lefkovitz, a strategist with Morningstar Indexes. "They've drawn parallels to the dotcom era and railroads and every other transformative technology build-out we've seen."Those concerns aren't likely to dissipate anytime soon. The 10 largest companies in the S&P 500 currently command 37% of the index, and 37% of the benchmark's weighting is in tech stocks as of Nov. 17. That is before Anthropic's initial public offering, which could add another major AI player to the top of the market. While the firm won't immediately join the S&P 500, it's reportedly targeting a valuation that would make it the tenth-largest publicly traded U.S. firm on the market when it begins trading. A market that's top-heavy and heavily tilted toward a single industry doesn't a bubble make. Historically, market bubbles have come when the price investors will pay for a particular investment becomes disconnected from its underlying value — and the jury is still out on whether that's the case for major AI stocks. But if the idea that a major chunk of your portfolio revolves around a single technology is keeping you up at night, it may make sense to adjust your strategy, financial experts say. Here's how. Nervous investors: Focus on diversificationIf you're worried about a potential bubble bursting, your first step is to evaluate your portfolio's exposures, says Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at financial services firm Ameriprise. "You want to make sure you're diversified, and that not all of your eggs are in tech or the AI theme," he says, adding that, after years of outperformance, tech firms make up a huge portion of many passively managed, market-capitalization-weighted index funds. "That works well when tech is going well. It doesn't work right now when tech is having a sell-off."If you determine you want to dial back your exposure to AI and technology names, however, the smart move isn't to take your ball and go home, says Lefkovitz. Rather, he says, you'd be wise to maintain your exposure to stocks while broadening what your portfolio holds. "Exiting the market is an extreme option," he says. "People have been talking about the market being overvalued or too tech-heavy, too AI-heavy for years now. And if you had exited, you would have missed out on some tremendous gains."So consider tweaking your portfolio at the margins, he suggests. That may mean adding exposure to an equal-weight version of your favorite index, rather than one that holds bigger companies in bigger quantities. You could also tilt towards indexes that track international stocks or smaller U.S.-based companies — both of which are less exposed to tech and AI names. The same general idea applies to dividend strategies and ones that focus on undervalued stocks, which tend to skew toward older-economy firms. No matter which route you consider, be sure to talk with a trusted financial advisor before making any wholesale moves in your portfolio. The goal, says Lefkovitz, isn't to upend your strategy or abandon AI or tech altogether, but to dial things down to a level that you're comfortable with. "There are ways to participate [in the stock market] without being so reliant on the top end of the market and that AI theme," he says. But remember: Volatility is the price of admissionYou could examine your portfolio and find that you're entirely comfortable with your exposure to AI. Even with tech in turmoil, many market watchers see a persistent demand for AI infrastructure, such as microchips and data centers, and have faith that so-called hyperscalers — megacap tech firms such as Alphabet and Microsoft — will reap huge future profits from the current AI buildout. While the current environment presents the risk of a short-term drawdown, younger investors hoping to cash in on AI should focus on the long-term opportunity the technology presents, says Jamie Cox, managing partner for financial planning firm Harris Financial Group. "If you're Gen Z and you're worried about a tech bubble, you're not thinking about this right," he says. Those with decades to invest should be comfortable with the short-term ups and downs of the stock market because they have plenty of time to let fallen markets recover and ascend higher, he says: "Time is on your side."Historically, the U.S. stock market has trended upward, rewarding investors who were willing to buy and hold stocks. That's not always an easy proposition in the short term, notes Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group, a wealth management firm. Broad-market pullbacks of 5% or more happen more than three times per year, on average, with drawdowns of 10% or more happening about once a year, he notes. "Every year you're going to have volatility, and it's uncomfortable. But volatility is the toll we pay to invest," he says. "If you want the joys of longer-term stock returns over decades, you're going to have some very uncomfortable moments along the way."

schema.headline: Worried about the AI bubble popping? How investing pros say to adjust your strategy

title: Mortgage demand turns lower, as interest rates shoot back up to the highest level in three weeks
description: A for sale sign is posted in front of a home for sale, Nov. 12, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesMor
body: A for sale sign is posted in front of a home for sale, Nov. 12, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesMortgage demand had been improving, as interest rates fell for about a month, but that came to an abrupt end last week. Mortgage rates moved sharply higher, causing total mortgage application volume to drop 2.3% from the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index. The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, increased last week to 7.35% from 7.21%, with points rising to 0.79 from 0.75, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment. That was its highest rate in three weeks."Treasury yields rose last week amid data showing inflation accelerated in October and Fed officials acknowledging that additional rate hikes may be needed in the coming months," said Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist at the MBA. Applications to refinance a home loan fell 2% for the week and were 54% lower than the same week one year ago. While overall refinance activity declined, Federal Housing Administration refinances increased almost 7%. The FHA offers low-down-payment government loans at lower interest rates but requires borrowers to pay mortgage insurance."The FHA rate was roughly 30 basis points below the conforming rate, which supported refinance opportunities for some homeowners," added Kan.Get Property Play directly to your inboxCNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox.Subscribe here to get access today.Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home fell 3% for the week and were 18% below where they were one year ago. Potential buyers are dealing with both affordability challenges as well as weaker confidence in the overall economy due to persistent inflation. Mortgage rates haven't done much to start this week, staying essentially flat, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily. There is more housing data set to be released this week with the Census report on monthly housing starts and building permits, as well as the monthly pending home sales index from the National Association of Realtors.

schema.headline: Mortgage demand turns lower, as interest rates shoot back up to the highest level in three weeks

title: Iran says army targets U.S. drone and missile sites in Kuwait as Gulf attacks mount
description: KHABARI AL AWAZEEM, KUWAIT - DECEMBER 18:  The final section of the last American military convoy to depart Iraq from the 3rd Brigade, 1st Cavalry Div
body: KHABARI AL AWAZEEM, KUWAIT - DECEMBER 18:  The final section of the last American military convoy to depart Iraq from the 3rd Brigade, 1st Cavalry Division crosses over the border into Kuwait on December 18, 2011 in Khabari Al Awazeem, Kuwait. Mario Tama | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesIran said its army targeted U.S. drone and missile installations at Kuwait's Ali Al Salem air base, according to local media, extending a series of attacks on Gulf states hosting American forces.Kuwait's army said on Tuesday evening that its air defenses had countered hostile drone attacks, without providing further details.Tensions between Iran and the U.S. have escalated sharply in recent days as strikes resumed across the Middle East, even as diplomatic talks continued.Bahrain has also sustained a wave of Iranian drone strikes, issuing an "all-clear" alert on Wednesday after its air defenses intercepted several aerial threats. Iran has previously claimed attacks on U.S. radar systems in Bahrain.CNN reported late Monday that U.S. intelligence found Iran was developing plans that could involve a so-called dirty bomb to target Washington, D.C. The administration officials, including President Donald Trump, have played down any imminent threat while saying the government continues to monitor the situation.Speaking at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila, Philippines, Trump warned that Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before" if such a plan existed.Secretary of State Marco Rubio echoed Trump's comments when addressing reporters in Manila, saying he did not see any imminent threats to the U.S. capital, but that the government is "always on the lookout for anything that's a threat."Trump nodded and said, "We are looking into it," while adding, "We are doing very well in Iran."The renewed attacks come as diplomatic efforts to end the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, now in its ninth month, appear to be stalled, while disruptions continue to weigh on energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz.Crude futures settled lower amid signs of recovering oil flows through the critical waterway. The International Energy Agency said Friday that the global oil supply had surpassed demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war and projected the market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter.The U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures dropped 1.2% to $84.9 a barrel, while Brent was down 0.48% at $92.7 per barrel.

schema.headline: Iran says army targets U.S. drone and missile sites in Kuwait as Gulf attacks mount

title: Senators press acting U.S. Navy Secretary on Iran war costs, sailor health in confirmation hearing
description: WASHINGTON, DC - NOVEMBER 17: Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao testifies during a confirmation hearing in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on N
body: WASHINGTON, DC - NOVEMBER 17: Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao testifies during a confirmation hearing in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on November 17, 2026 in Washington, DC. Cao, nominated by President Trump, faced questions about the Iran War. (Photo by Finn Gomez/Getty Images)Finn Gomez | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesActing U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao's confirmation hearing before the Senate Armed Services Committee led to some heated exchanges as he was grilled about sailors' health and the Iran war.The Navy changed condition codes on munitions previously classified as expired in order to use them, Cao told senators Tuesday, as lawmakers questioned the conflict's strain on weapons stocks and naval deployments. He also said the military had increased production of key weapons."When I was in uniform, we only produced 125 Tomahawks a year. Right now, we're well above 60 every month," he said, adding that the military was working to increase SM-6 missile production and bring in additional ammunition manufacturers.Cao's confirmation hearing comes as the Republicans, who hold a majority in both the House and Senate, are coming to the end of their time in power in both houses. The Democratic Party flipped many seats in the midterm elections to win a comfortable majority in the next session starting in January. President Donald Trump's nominees for offices, and his legislative agenda, will face much tougher challenges then.Cao said the Navy was accelerating work on unmanned surface vessels to relieve the 17 destroyers supporting the blockade of Iran's ships, in hopes of reducing the strain on the Fifth Fleet. But Senators still pointed to the war's effect on the Navy's resources."For the first time in many years, the United States has no forward-deployed carrier in the Pacific at this moment," Sen. Jack Reed (D-R.I.) noted.Cao acknowledged that the war was "stressing our naval resources." However, he argued that the demonstration of combined American military capabilities had "really set China back on their heels," a characterization Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) disputed.Lawmakers also pressed Cao on the war's financial costs, with Cao appearing to agree with Sen. Elizabeth Warren's (D-Mass.) estimate of approximately $32.5 million a day in costs to maintain the blockade on Iranian ports. The demands of prolonged deployments have raised concerns about sailors' access to food and basic supplies, as Cao told senators that the destroyer USS Gonzalez had a week of rations remaining."Usually, I don't like them to go below two weeks of supplies," he said, while insisting the provisions were adequate and ships had never run out of food.When Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) asked about reports of sailors losing 45 pounds, Cao stated that the food preferences might not be to certain sailors' liking.He likened it to his children opening the refrigerator door and saying "there's nothing to eat here.""Losing 45 pounds is more serious than just not liking the food. Our sailors are being asked to serve thousands of miles from home for months at a time. We have a responsibility to make sure they have what they need to do their jobs and stay healthy," Kelly posted on X.Senators also questioned Cao about eight suicide attempts across the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group during its deployment. Cao defended the Navy's mental health support, describing the incidents as "eight suicide mitigations" because personnel had intervened.Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.) called the term "mitigations" an "insult," saying they should be called suicide attempts.The questioning followed an earlier acknowledgment by the top U.S. commander in the Middle East of mental health concerns aboard the Lincoln.Cao pledged that the entire Department of the Navy would achieve a clean financial audit by the end of the fiscal year. The Pentagon has had nine consecutive failures to obtain a clean department-wide audit opinion, according to Reuters."We owe the American public to tell them exactly where their money is," he said.If you are having thoughts of suicide, please know that you are not alone. If you are in danger of acting on suicidal thoughts, call 911. If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. Call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.

schema.headline: Senators press acting U.S. Navy Secretary on Iran war costs, sailor health in confirmation hearing

title: IEA chief sees no 'credible pathway' back to pre-war normality in the Strait of Hormuz
description: Fatih Birol, executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), at the Semafor World Economy Summit during the International Monetary Fund (
body: Fatih Birol, executive director of the International Energy Agency (IEA), at the Semafor World Economy Summit during the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Spring meetings in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, April 14, 2026.Bloomberg | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Iran war has "crushed" confidence in the Strait of Hormuz as a reliable supply corridor, IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol warned.IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote in an article published Wednesday that he was skeptical of a return to "normalization.""I don't see any credible pathway back to the situation that existed in February 2026," Birol wrote in a guest essay for The Economist's "The World Ahead 2027," published Wednesday."Shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz have been blocked once, with a hugely disruptive effect on oil and gas markets. It can happen again. Confidence in the Strait as a safe and reliable corridor for energy and other goods has been crushed," he said.Before the war began on Feb. 28, the strait was a major artery for oil and gas. Gulf crude exports have recovered in recent months, reaching more than 80% of pre-war levels in October, the IEA said in its November market report. But renewed U.S.-Iran strikes broke a lull in direct fighting this week."I think perceptions of risk around the Strait have changed for good," Birol added, citing new routes, such as pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates that bypass the strait.At 6:45 a.m. ET, U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were seen trading at $85 a barrel, with international benchmark Brent crude futures at $92.74 a barrel.'Uncertainty is now the rule' Many IEA members relied on emergency oil stocks, softening the economic disruptions, Birol wrote.Southeast Asian countries such as the Philippines and Thailand are looking to "build up similar buffers," as they were the hardest hit by the energy shock, he added.Birol predicted that the crisis would accelerate countries' shift toward domestic energy sources such as cost-competitive solar and wind, while renewing interest in nuclear power.But this will require stronger grids and battery storage, he added."Uncertainty is now the rule, not the exception, so energy decision-makers need to be wary of creating new dependencies, even as they seek to address old ones," Birol said.

schema.headline: IEA chief sees no 'credible pathway' back to pre-war normality in the Strait of Hormuz

title: China’s military seeks Nvidia’s advanced chips for AI capabilities, commission says
description: Dado Ruvic | ReutersChina's People's Liberation Army has been "actively soliciting" Nvidia's most advanced semiconductor chips to develop its artifici
body: Dado Ruvic | ReutersChina's People's Liberation Army has been "actively soliciting" Nvidia's most advanced semiconductor chips to develop its artificial intelligence-enabled military capabilities, a congressional commission said in a report released Wednesday.The report comes as Nvidia has been rocked by the resignation of its CEO, Jensen Huang, after reports that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who worked for Singapore-based Megaspeed, which is being eyed by U.S. investigators for potential diversion of Nvidia's chips to China."China is seeking to evade U.S. export controls to gain the most advanced semiconductors that underpin its intelligentization drive," the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission said in its 2026 annual report to Congress.China is making that move as it faces a quality gap between chips produced by Chinese companies, including Huawei and Cambricon, and the more advanced ones produced by Nvidia and other U.S. companies, such as Advanced Micro Devices, the report noted.The report's findings could fuel concerns about advanced Nvidia chips having found their way to Chinese users amid escalating investigations from Congress and state and federal regulators."Although China has made some progress in achieving its goals, it has not yet closed the hardest chokepoints — including the most advanced capabilities in logic fabrication, memory, and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, as well as the Nvidia Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA) software moat — and likely will not for some time," the report said."The resulting gap in compute is substantial, largely due to U.S. export controls on advanced chips," the report said.The report highlighted the fact that in the meantime, Chinese companies have obtained remote access to Nvidia chips through data centers in third countries, including Malaysia.On Tuesday, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued a rule intended to cut off that workaround.The move came in response to criticism from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Congress members that the Commerce Department had not done enough to prevent Nvidia's most advanced chips from being diverted to China in violation of U.S. export controls.The U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission was created by Congress in 2000 with a mandate to monitor and report to Congress the national security implications of the trade and economic relationship between the U.S. and China.

schema.headline: China’s military seeks Nvidia’s advanced chips for AI capabilities, commission says

title: Tech outages are causing people to panic-buy. Costco is benefiting, Mizuho says
description: A shopper leaves a Costco store in Bayonne, New Jersey, Oct. 2, 2026.Gary Hershorn | Corbis News | Getty ImagesA series of tech outages has consumers
body: A shopper leaves a Costco store in Bayonne, New Jersey, Oct. 2, 2026.Gary Hershorn | Corbis News | Getty ImagesA series of tech outages has consumers stocking up on emergency supplies.Costco sales are seeing a lift because of it, according to research firm Mizuho.In the final week of October, Mizuho estimates, Costco's U.S. comparable sales, excluding gasoline, rose 11% to 12%, up from the normal 6% to 7% the first three weeks in October. Costco reported an 8.1% increase for the month. The firm said the stronger pace is continuing through November, as 21 of the 26 high-ticket generators it tracked on Costco's website sold out as of Sunday night.Shares of Costco were roughly flat-to-lower in Wednesday morning trading at around $1,107 apiece."Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at COST," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger said in a research note Monday. Bellinger will appear on CNBC's "The Exchange" during the 1 p.m. hour.On Thursday, an outage occurred in Microsoft's Outlook and Teams, and on Friday the Federal Aviation Administration halted departures nationwide. On Monday, a software outage at JPMorgan Chase caused banking transaction delays, and a system outage delayed United Airlines flights. The National Security Agency said Tuesday that the spy agency's communication network went down temporarily.The outages appear to come amid a rush to recover software vulnerabilities uncovered by AI tools, and officials are saying there's no reason for panic.Still, on TikTok and other social media platforms, posts urging people to stock up on food and supplies are gaining significant traction.Mizuho raised its price target on Costco to $1,150 from $1,100 and kept its buy-equivalent outperform rating. The firm said U.S. comparable sales could grow more than 10% in November. Mizuho also sees Walmart's Sam's Club benefiting from emergency preparedness sales as shoppers fill up their pantries, and for Home Depot and Lowe's as they buy home improvement emergency supplies.At Costco, Mizuho will be watching whether the surge brought in new member sign-ups when the warehouse retailer reports its first quarter of fiscal 2027 on Dec. 10.

schema.headline: Tech outages are causing people to panic-buy. Costco is benefiting, Mizuho says

title: U.S. soldier taken into military custody over suspected spying for Russia
description: Quavondo | E+ | Getty ImagesLONDON — The American military has taken a U.S. Army soldier into custody after he was arrested in the U.K. on suspicion o
body: Quavondo | E+ | Getty ImagesLONDON — The American military has taken a U.S. Army soldier into custody after he was arrested in the U.K. on suspicion of spying for Russia, British authorities said Tuesday evening. Senior serviceman Lt. Col. Brandon Carroll Tyner was arrested in England last week as part of an investigation by Britain's Counter Terrorism Policing with assistance from U.S. authorities, including the military and the FBI.He was assigned to the NATO military alliance's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC) and stationed at its headquarters in the county of Gloucestershire, working in human resources. ARRC has more than 400 permanent staff from more than 20 nations ready to deploy land forces where they are needed.The U.S. Army confirmed Tyner's identity to CNBC on Wednesday. Moscow denies involvementFollowing his arrest, the 41-year-old was detained in London on suspicion of committing offenses under Sections 1 and 3 of the U.K.'s National Security Act.Authorities did not share details of the case, but Section 1 offenses relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while Section 3 covers assisting a foreign intelligence service.CNBC reached out to the Russian government for comment on the latest developments in the case. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Nov. 11 that Moscow had "absolutely nothing to do with" the situation, following the soldier's arrest.British prosecutors engaged with the U.K. Attorney General's Office and American partners after what U.K. officials called "an extensive investigation."A decision was then made to pass the investigation to U.S. authorities, in line with international protocol. U.S. vows justice FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement on Tuesday that the service has "zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk."U.S. Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon said in a statement that the case should serve as a "stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the Constitution." "Whenever we suspect somebody of betraying the trust of their fellow soldiers and jeopardizing our collective defense, we will identify you, and we will ensure justice is served," he said. "These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place," Laurence Taylor, head of the U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing, said as the updates on the case were announced. "We will continue to support our U.S. colleagues as they take the matter forwards," he added.

schema.headline: U.S. soldier taken into military custody over suspected spying for Russia

title: Jeffries wins Democratic House speaker race, on track to make history in January
description: U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 17, 2026.Brendan Smialow
body: U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 17, 2026.Brendan Smialowski | Afp | Getty ImagesHouse Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won the nod from his caucus to become the next speaker of the House of Representatives. Jeffries, D-N.Y., still needs to be officially elected when the new Congress convenes in January. But he appears to be on a glide path to winning the gavel after Democrats voted 251-11 to nominate him, according to a person familiar with the vote who spoke on condition of anonymity to describe the private meeting. The win for Jeffries comes after months of acrimony over whether Democrats would stand by their existing leadership or oust them amid a progressive tide. Democrats trounced Republicans in the midterm elections and are poised to hold at least 257 House seats. Jeffries would make history as the first Black speaker of the House if he is elected in January.

schema.headline: Jeffries wins Democratic House speaker race, on track to make history in January

title: Two new housing reports point to bleak winter ahead, with record low sales
description: Single-family homes in Miami, Florida, Aug. 1, 2025.Joe Raedle | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesTwo new reports on the housing market show activity s
body: Single-family homes in Miami, Florida, Aug. 1, 2025.Joe Raedle | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesTwo new reports on the housing market show activity slowing even more, after a September spike in mortgage rates sent it into a deep freeze.Pending home sales in October dropped 4.7% month-over-month and were down 16.7% from October of last year, according to the National Association of Realtors. This is the lowest level in the index's 25-year history.Analysts had been looking for a much smaller decline, likely because mortgage rates pulled back slightly in October, only to rise sharply again last week. The average rate on the 30-year fixed started October at 7.54% according to Mortgage News Daily and ended the month at 7.27%.The pending count is based on signed contracts — people out shopping and signing deals during the month. It is therefore an indicator of future closed sales. "Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s," said Lawrence Yun, NAR's chief economist in a release.Regionally, sales were down across the nation with the sharpest drops in the South, which is usually busiest for sales and the West which is most expensive.Another report released Wednesday showed gains in home construction in October but raised a red flag going forward. Single-family housing starts rose 4% from September, according to the U.S. Census, but were down 3.2% year over year. Building permits, an indicator of future construction, dropped 8.7% for the month and were down 12.9% from October 2025. That is the lowest level for permits since May 2020, the start of the Covid-19 pandemic."Builders are dealing with a litany of obstacles to selling homes, whether it's rising costs of land, labor, and materials, high financing costs, or weak buyer demand," wrote Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com. "This month's data shows them slowing down activity at the top of their funnel, which will result in slower months of starts and completions later on."The construction report follows a bleak reading on homebuilder sentiment, which fell to the lowest level in 14 years in November, on the monthly index from the National Association of Home Builders. Builders cited multiple challenges, including higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and labor, as well as weaker consumer confidence.Get Property Play directly to your inboxCNBC's Property Play with Diana Olick covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, delivered weekly to your inbox.Subscribe here to get access today.

schema.headline: Two new housing reports point to bleak winter ahead, with record low sales

title: Democrat Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate election
description: Democrat senatorial candidate Mary Peltola speaks during a midterm election night party at the Sheraton Anchorage in Anchorage, Alaska on November 3,
body: Democrat senatorial candidate Mary Peltola speaks during a midterm election night party at the Sheraton Anchorage in Anchorage, Alaska on November 3, 2026. Charly Triballeau | Afp | Getty ImagesDemocratic candidate Mary Peltola won the Alaska Senate election, capping a midterm cycle that already was one of the best for Democrats in more than a half-century, the Associated Press reported Tuesday evening.Peltola defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in a race that was surrounded by controversy over an independent candidate who shared his name. Peltola had faced accusations that her campaign recruited ultra-longshot candidate Dan J. Sullivan to the race to confuse voters. The Justice Department filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the election if the incumbent Sullivan lost in order to conduct an investigation into whether voter confusion tainted the outcome.The Justice Department is appealing the dismissal of that civil suit. The department is also conducting a criminal investigation into the second Sullivan's decision to enter the race.Peltola's victory gives Democrats a solid majority of 56 seats in the Senate beginning in January.Democrats this cycle flipped nine Senate seats that are currently held by Republicans.That outcome, which was not considered remotely likely at the beginning of the election, came as part of a massive Democratic wave this year, which saw the party also flip majority control of the House of Representatives by a decisive margin.Alaska was the last Senate race to be called in the midterm elections. Peltola, a former House member, joins Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan as the first two Native American women elected to the Senate.The race was called two weeks after Election Day, and six days after Peltola's fellow Democrat Scott Colom pulled off perhaps the most stunning upset of the 2026 cycle by defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi Senate race.As of 10:39 p.m. ET, Peltola had 50.1% of the vote, and Sullivan had 45.8%. Another Republican, Gerald Heikes, had 2.1% of the vote, while Daniel J. Sullivan had 1.6% of the vote.If no candidate exceeded 50% of the vote, the election would have been decided through a ranked-choice method, in which the two bottom finishers would have been eliminated, and the second choices on the ballots of voters who selected them would be allocated to the remaining two candidates."From Juneau to Utqiagvik, the message from Alaskans is clear: the status quo in DC is not working for Alaska," Peltola said in a statement."Over the course of this campaign I've spoken with elders in tears about empty fish racks; families struggling to find housing they can afford; and parents in the Bush faced with the impossible choice of heating their homes or putting food on the table," Peltola said. "Today we take a monumental step forward in addressing those issues and putting Alaska first."As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans' support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," she said. "Thank you Alaska. Let's get to work."

schema.headline: Democrat Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate election

title: Target shares rise 5% as retailer posts best sales growth in five years, hikes guidance
description: Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnar
body: Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnaround strategy taking hold.The retailer said its net sales grew 7.1% during the fiscal third quarter. Comparable sales rose 5.6%, compared with StreetAccount estimates of up 3.8%. That growth was boosted by a 5% increase in comparable traffic, Target added. "[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters. Digital comparable sales jumped nearly 10% during the quarter.Encouraged by the growth, Target raised its full-year guidance, upping its net sales growth guidance by 1 percentage point to around 6%. It's also expecting full-year operating income margin rate to be around 6.2%, which includes roughly 1.1 percentage points of benefit from tariff refunds.The company also said it's now projecting full-year earnings per share to be in a range of $10.65 to $11.40, compared with prior guidance of between $9.90 and $10.90. "The changes we've made across our assortment and guest experience are adding up," Fiddelke told reporters. "While we're encouraged by the progress, we know there's more work ahead to sustain this momentum and deliver consistent growth over time."Target shares climbed more than 5% in morning trading Wednesday.Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: $2.65 vs. $2.07 expectedRevenue: $27.07 billion vs. $26.56 billion expectedFor the quarter ended Oct. 31, Target reported net income of $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, up from $689 million, or $1.51 per share, a year earlier. This year, the company said it's invested approximately $3.8 billion in capital expenditures, up nearly $1 billion from last year. Because of those returns, Fiddelke said Target is now expecting to invest between $5 billion and $6 billion in capex next year. On a call with analysts, he added that those investments will go toward more store remodels, technology, supply chain improvements, among other initiatives.The company said it saw particular strength in beauty, which saw 9% growth, and food and beverage, where sales increased nearly 7%. The retailer added that net sales rose in all three months of the third quarter, with the strongest performance during the back-to-school season. Fiddelke told reporters the quarter's strength showed "continued progress" toward Target's priorities that it outlined at the beginning of its turnaround. As it looks to the holiday season, Target said it's marketing thousands of products priced at $5 and under, along with new artificial intelligence-powered shopping experiences to drive engagement. Fiddelke said Target is "encouraged" by shopping behaviors it's seen so far in the current quarter.The big-box retailer has been showing signs of returning to growth, as it sees stronger sales trends after years of flat revenue. The results come after Target last quarter hiked its full fiscal-year outlook and said it saw "broad-based" strength across its various categories.It's also lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in an effort to get customers back into its stores, especially as consumer sentiment lags and inflation remains high. The retailer said on Wednesday that it cut prices on an additional roughly 2,000 items during the third quarter.Target's stock is up more than 70% this year.

schema.headline: Target shares rise 5% as retailer posts best sales growth in five years, hikes guidance

title: I watched Trump, Xi and Putin gather in China. Here are my top takeaways
description: US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and China’s President Xi Jinping attend a photo session before the welcome banquet at the
body: US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and China’s President Xi Jinping attend a photo session before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, southern China, November 18, 2026. Iori Sagisawa | Via ReutersSHENZHEN, China — It took a trip to China for me, an American, to see U.S. President Donald Trump in person for the first time. Trump emerged from a group of black-clad photographers and other personnel surrounding him at a welcome banquet in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Leaders' Meeting held November 17th to 19th.Seated just a few spots to his left was Russian President Vladimir Putin who picked up a glass of red wine to join a toast led by Chinese President Xi Jinping."At tomorrow's Leaders' Meeting, we will discuss measures to expand mutual opening up, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, and identify opportunities to expand practical cooperation across various fields, so as to translate more initiatives into tangible results," Xi said in Mandarin, according to a CNBC translation.Xi was speaking broadly, but Thursday's agenda includes a bilateral meeting with Trump, and their highly anticipated trilateral meeting with Putin. But looking at the mood in the room, it seemed that their trilateral conversation had already started Wednesday night at their long banquet table. Much of what happens at APEC, including bilateral meetings and other exchanges between leaders, takes place away from the media.But what struck me was how little sign there was of the tension surrounding Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang resignation, a controversy that has gripped markets for the past 10 days.Ahead of Trump's entrance into the banquet hall, Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao shared a friendly moment with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other members of the American delegation.U.S. and China trade negotiators chatted on the sidelines of a welcome banquet for APEC economic leaders in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18, 2026.CNBC | Evelyn ChengLast week, the U.S. officials said that Trump did not plan to raise allegations of Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy during his meeting with Xi. It was a striking contrast to just two months ago, when I saw photographs of Huang and Tesla CEO Elon Musk sharing a table with Trump and Xi in Washington, D.C.And when Trump visited Beijing in May, Huang took a few minutes to speak with reporters, including me, inside the Great Hall of the People. Musk was there too, accompanied by one of his sons.This time, neither were visible in a room that was closely watched by the world. Musk was expected to join Trump's delegation in Shenzhen, but I did not see him Wednesday evening.Their absence from the government-heavy banquet was striking. The world's most powerful leaders may be grappling with the implications of artificial intelligence, but they certainly didn't need the industry's biggest names at the table to do so.Over the months I've spent following APEC's "China Year," one thing has become clear: The forum has given Beijing an opportunity to host the U.S., Japan and other member economies at a time when unresolved tensions might otherwise have made such gatherings difficult.But even in a year defined by talks of U.S.-China "strategic stability," the APEC events have exposed the rifts and the shifting dynamics in global power. Those dynamics were on display for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit. Several hundred attendees, from Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun to U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue, arrived early for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit. After waiting in silence for at least 10 minutes, the audience welcomed Xi in a distinctly modern way: by raising their smartphones to capture the moment. The applause was rather muted.It was much the same at the more government-heavy welcome banquet that evening. So many attendees rushed to take their own photographs of Xi and other leaders entering the room that reporters' views were largely blocked.Chinese President Xi Jinping gave an opening speech Wednesday for the APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18, 2026.CNBC | Evelyn ChengFollowing Xi's morning speech, there was a lengthy intermission before Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim took the stage."The entire multilateral framework needs to change," he said, praising China on its "rare" recognition of smaller countries.During the tea break that followed, attendees quickly resumed mingling. Some even brought coffee and snacks back into the room as Putin prepared to speak. They listened as the Russian president talked about his country's economic resilience and claimed Europe was losing ground. As attendees headed to lunch, one thing stood out: Neither Trump nor any other G7 leader had taken the stage at the opening event. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke later in the afternoon.The most visible American presence during the morning session came from business leaders appearing in a promotional video ahead of Xi's speech.And the absence of an American voice was perhaps even more noticeable at Wednesday evening's banquet. Trump did not follow Xi with a toast of his own. This was the same famously outspoken president, who in a winding speech in Davos, had declared that the U.S. must get Greenland. Yet on Wednesday night in China, Trump wasn't the one holding the microphone.

schema.headline: I watched Trump, Xi and Putin gather in China. Here are my top takeaways

title: Lowe's posts strong online sales, raises outlook despite slow housing market
description: Lowe's on Wednesday posted strong quarterly results and raised its full-year outlook as the company said it saw strength among professional shoppers.T
body: Lowe's on Wednesday posted strong quarterly results and raised its full-year outlook as the company said it saw strength among professional shoppers.The company said comparable sales grew 1.8% for the fiscal third quarter, driven by a 17.4% increase in online sales and "solid" performance in pro and home services sales. Net sales rose to $22.76 billion.Because of the strength, Lowe's now said it expects full-year sales of roughly $92.5 billion, up from a previous projection of $92 billion. It also expects comparable sales to be up 0.5%, compared with previous guidance of flat.CEO Marvin Ellison told CNBC that the company is focused on growing despite economic headwinds and a sluggish housing market. He said Lowe's posted its sixth straight quarterly comparable sales increase and saw particular strength in appliances, which saw its largest revenue growth in five years."We believe irrespective of the macro environment we're in, we're going to take share because there's a lot of share out there that we can go and get, and we're going to be aggressive to go and get that share," Ellison told CNBC.Lowe's also reported a pretax benefit of approximately $250 million from tariff refunds during the quarter, which contributed a 34-cent boost to earnings per share. Ellison said the company plans to use those funds to enhance the customer experience and bring value to shoppers.He added that do-it-yourself customers and pro shoppers are not investing in major renovation projects but are instead spending on repair and maintenance projects. "We are giving those pros what they need," he said. "We're able to improve our fulfillment capabilities and our pro loyalty program."Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: $3.10 adjusted, it was not immediately clear if that compared to the $2.88 expectedRevenue: $22.76 billion vs. $22.41 billion expectedFor the quarter ended Oct. 30, Lowe's reported net income of $1.67 billion, or $2.98 per share, compared with $1.62 billion, or $2.88 per share, the year prior.The home improvement retailer has previously said it's seeing "pressure" on spending on projects, especially as consumers are stretched thin by inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty. The company is also battling a slower housing market and higher mortgage rates. Ellison previously told CNBC he expects consumers to remain cautious through the end of the year. Lowe's executives said on a call with analysts Wednesday that the company is continuing to battle high fuel costs, which they said accelerated through the third quarter. CFO Brandon Sink said diesel prices are currently around $6 per gallon, up about 15% overall compared to what the company saw in the second quarter."So we're trying to continue to manage that, balance that, and we're reflecting that into our Q4 guide," Sink said. Ellison told CNBC the company remains optimistic about consumer spending this holiday season and that November sales are in line with expectations so far. Lowe's competitor Home Depot said earlier this week that it's seeing resilience among professional shoppers and reported comparable sales growth.

schema.headline: Lowe's posts strong online sales, raises outlook despite slow housing market

title: Vance scraps schedule to address tech outages as Trump admin insists incidents aren't linked
description: Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday abruptly canceled his scheduled appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit to instead attend meetings on a
body: Vice President JD Vance on Wednesday abruptly canceled his scheduled appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit to instead attend meetings on a recent wave of high-profile technology outages.The cancellation was announced shortly after a senior Trump administration official insisted that the outages, which have affected a wide range of industries and have been felt across the country and around the world, are not the result of a cyberattack or any form of coordinated action.Samuel Boivin | Nurphoto | Getty Images"We have a great deal of confidence in our assessment that these incidents are the result of upgrades of the systems, systems being patched, hardware being applied" or other "disparate" events, the official said on condition of anonymity to discuss the government's intelligence assessments.The official briefed news outlets by phone in the wake of numerous major disruptions at large corporations and federal agencies in recent days, including a nationwide ground stop, a protracted Microsoft Outlook outage and a reported blackout of the National Security Agency's classified communications network.Other incidents include software issues at JPMorgan Chase, an outage at United Airlines that caused some flight delays and product issues at Apple.On Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC that the outages are not a cyberattack "not a coordinated effort by a nation state."He gave a similar assurance on Wednesday to the House Homeland Security Committee."We have no indication that these incidents are related, that they're coordinated," Clayton said. "We also have no indication that they're result of a state-sponsored malign actor."But the sheer volume of incidents in the past week alone has raised alarm bells among consumers and tech experts alike, with some wondering if rapidly advancing artificial intelligence models are to blame.The senior Trump administration official, asked on Wednesday's call to what degree AI was involved in the outages, said it is "challenging to answer that question across all of these incidents that have been reported."Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told CNBC Wednesday morning he wants "better coordination" on AI safety."I understand why people are freaked out," Warner said. "The one way we could lose this AI race and [see] all of these companies' valuations plummet dramatically is if we have an AI tool run amok, or an AI-sponsored cyberattack that creates harm."His comments came hours before before Anthropic is scheduled to price its initial public offering for the first major AI industry IPO.Warner advocated for a "pre-testing regime" for new AI models that establishes guardrails and helps ensure a "culture of safety built in" to the industry."He said the U.S. is "lucky" that it has so far avoided a major AI-generated cyberattack or a crisis with a rogue agent that goes beyond incidents like Hugging Face breach earlier this year.— CNBC's Samantha Subin contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Vance scraps schedule to address tech outages as Trump admin insists incidents aren't linked
